title: Cascaded vs speech-to-speech pipelines
summary: A cascaded (chained) pipeline runs speech-to-text, a text agent and text-to-speech as separate stages. A speech-to-speech model does it in one. The choice trades latency against control over the text in between.
useIf: You are choosing a voice architecture and must weigh latency, text inspection, tool-heavy backends, cost and platform limits.
avoidIf: You have a single fixed requirement that already decides it, such as a rule that no text may be stored, or a hard sub-second target.

explain.md: In a **chained pipeline** you manage three stages: speech-to-text, your agent workflow, and text-to-speech. Use it when you need to inspect or transform text between stages, for example to store the transcript, run policy checks before the agent answers, or speak only after an approved answer [[r3]]. In **speech-to-speech** one model hears and speaks. Foundry's voice-based agent docs describe the same split: native speech-to-speech is optimised for low latency, while cascaded gives more model and voice choice and control, but each stage adds latency [[r8]] (preview, checked 2026-10-13).

Two more shapes sit between them. **GPT-Live** is full duplex and delegates reasoning to a separate backend, so a slow tool call does not freeze the conversation [[r3]]. **Azure Voice Live** is a managed pipeline with noise suppression, echo cancellation and end-of-turn detection, available over WebSocket events close to the Realtime API [[r7]]. Whatever you pick, measure audible response time at the median and 95th percentile, task completion and interruption behaviour, and compare changes with the caller, prompt and transport held fixed [[r3]].

explain.title: Where you can intercept
explain.alt: The chained path has a policy check between speech-to-text and the text agent. The speech-to-speech path goes straight from the microphone to one model.

whereToUse: Regulated lines where transcripts must be stored or redacted before reasoning
Consumer assistants where latency and natural overlap matter most
Concierge agents whose backend calls internal systems and takes seconds
Azure estates that want Azure Speech features without hosting orchestration

use: Chained when text must be filtered or logged, or a tuned text agent already exists
Speech-to-speech when latency is the top priority
Delegation when a slow backend must not freeze the call
avoid: Speech-to-speech where a policy needs text before the model hears the audio
Chained when every stage adds latency you cannot afford and no text control is needed
Foundry voice agents in production if your policy forbids preview features
flips: A new rule demands transcript redaction: move from speech-to-speech to chained
Backend calls grow from 1 s to 6 s: add delegation or filler responses
The estate must be GA only: check the preview status of every voice component

pitfalls.symptom: Callers hear long silences in a chained agent
pitfalls.cause: Each stage waits for the previous one, and slow tools add up
pitfalls.fix: Stream between stages, add a short acknowledgment, and measure time to first audio at p95.

pitfalls.symptom: Compliance cannot show what the model heard
pitfalls.cause: A speech-to-speech session was chosen without a transcript or event log plan
pitfalls.fix: Log events and transcripts you are allowed to keep, or move to a chained design.

pitfalls.symptom: A 'one moment' filler arrives too late
pitfalls.cause: In Foundry voice agents `latency_threshold_ms` for interim responses defaults to 2000
pitfalls.fix: Lower it, as the docs advise [[r9]].

scenarios.title: Card-holder line with PII rules
scenarios.situation: A bank voice line must mask account numbers in the transcript before any model sees them, and keep an audit record of every utterance.
unknowns: Is a 1 to 2 second delay acceptable?
scenarios.question: Which architecture?

options.name: Chained pipeline with a redaction step between speech-to-text and the agent
options.why: Only a chained design lets you transform text before reasoning, and you store the transcript yourself [[r3]].
options.tradeoff: Added latency per stage and more components.

options.name: Realtime speech-to-speech with a policy prompt
options.why: The model hears raw audio, so a prompt cannot redact before it listens.
options.tradeoff: Right when no pre-model text control is needed.

options.name: GPT-Live with a text backend that redacts
options.why: The backend sees redacted text and holds the rules.
options.tradeoff: The live model still hears the raw audio, so it only fits if that is allowed.

flips.if: Policy allows the model to hear raw audio but forbids storing it
flips.then: Speech-to-speech with logging off becomes possible.

flips.if: Latency must be under a second
flips.then: Re-examine, since redaction forces a text stage.

scenarios.takeaway: Pre-model text control needs a text stage.

scenarios.title: Concierge with slow lookups
scenarios.situation: A hotel concierge agent calls booking and loyalty systems that take 4 to 8 seconds. Guests talk naturally and interrupt.
unknowns: Can the backend stream partial results?
scenarios.question: How do you keep the call alive?

options.name: GPT-Live with the existing workflow as the backend
options.why: Full duplex lets guests keep talking while the backend runs, and your logic stays in one place [[r3]].
options.tradeoff: Two prompts: speaking behaviour and business rules.

options.name: Realtime speech-to-speech with tool calls and a filler line
options.tradeoff: Tool waits still produce awkward pauses.

options.name: Chained pipeline
options.why: Adds stage latency on top of an already slow backend.
options.tradeoff: Right when text control outweighs responsiveness.

flips.then: Compare Voice Live with function calling.

scenarios.takeaway: Slow tools call for delegation or filler design.

quiz.q: Which new requirement most clearly forces a move from speech-to-speech to a chained pipeline?
options: Account numbers must be redacted before any model sees the text
The call must feel more natural
quiz.explain: Only a chained design lets you intercept and transform text between recognition and reasoning. Languages, naturalness and session length do not require a text stage.

quiz.q: Which statements fit the documented trade-off between native speech-to-speech and cascaded voice agents?
options: Native is optimised for low latency
Cascaded gives more model and voice choice and control
Cascaded removes all latency from each stage
Native lets you edit text between stages
quiz.explain: Foundry's docs say native is optimised for low latency and cascaded adds control at the cost of latency per stage. The other two statements are the reverse of that.

flashcards.front: When do you choose a chained voice pipeline?
flashcards.back: When you must inspect, redact, log or replace text between recognition, the agent and speech, or when a tuned text agent already exists.

flashcards.front: What problem does GPT-Live delegation solve?
flashcards.back: A slow backend freezing the call. The full-duplex live model keeps talking and listening while a separate backend does the reasoning.

flashcards.front: How do you compare voice architectures fairly?
flashcards.back: Hold caller, prompt, backend and transport fixed. Measure audible response time at p50 and p95, task completion, interruptions and unwanted silence.
